newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Gas users only clear winners of single EU market.
newsitem.headline: Gas users only clear winners of single EU market.

text.p: Despite widespread calls for gas market liberalisation, end users will be the only clear beneficiaries, the European Gas 97 conference heard on Tuesday.
Would-be investors and the industry itself had better beware. Even users themselves have no guarantee of gains after the first few years.
At least in the short term, the benefits for the customer appear clear, Patrick Lambert, head of the Gas Unit at the European Commission, told an audience of gas industry heads.
"In the UK, gas prices to industrial consumers have dropped by 55 percent since liberalisation," he said.
A Commission study says that customers in Europe too would reap large cost savings.
"In Europe, limited competition would result in savings of around 900 million ecu per annum, while increased competition would result in savings of 1.4 billion ecu or more," Lambert said.

However, the intense competition that seems likely offers neither investors nor industry a reliable return, at least according to Rod Mclean, director of oil and gas research at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
"The key question for investors is: will growth in gas demand more than offset the margin pressure," he said.
"An investor must be aware that somebody has to pay the bill for lower end user gas prices," he added.
His comments were echoed by Peter Mellbye, executive vice-president of Statoil.
"Low prices...will lead to some damage to shareholder value," he said.

Clearly monopolies offer investors an easier investment choice, but competition is Europe's chosen route. Mclean therefore urges governments to unbundle their gas utilities -- i.e. separate them vertically -- from the outset.
"Deregulation needn't be a painful experience, but it does require that the industry adopts the appropriate structure to begin with. This wasn't done in the UK," Mclean said.

The UK experience of electricity and water companies suggest that, despite talk of unbundling, the large players survive at the expense of the minnows and the ties, vertical and horizontal, are re-established, possibly at the expense of the customer.
For Dieter Helm, director of Oxford Energy Researh Associates, some rebundling appears inevitable, and regulation is the only way to ensure competition.
"It is hopeless to imagine that in an energy market without regulation, that anything other than monopoly would emerge.... Competition is not a spontaneous event," he said.

The appropriate regulatory body is, he says, the European Commission, but he questions whether individual nations are willing to transfer such powers. He is therefore pessimistic that a truly liberalised market will emerge.
The view is not shared by the European Commission.

"The Gas Directive is long overdue and, more importantly, the time is now ripe....Change is inevitable. The directive should ensure a level playing field...(and) we have grounds for optimism that we will soon succeed in our efforts," said Lamber of the European Commission.
-- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 5040 5004
